analysis.one_liner: Repeals corporate income taxes and estate taxes and replaces all individual income taxes with a flat 10% tax on wages only.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote, and died on the Senate calendar when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the corporate income tax, the estate tax, and the gift tax, and would replace today's individual income tax with a single 10% tax. But the tax would apply only to earned income — paychecks and self-employment earnings — while capital gains, interest, rents, most dividends, and pensions would go completely untaxed. Every existing deduction and credit, from the standard deduction to the child credit, would be repealed and replaced by a $10,000-per-person exemption, indexed to inflation.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations would pay no income tax at all. Households living on investments — capital gains, interest, rents, most dividends, and pensions — would owe essentially nothing. Large estates would pass to heirs tax-free. People earning wages would pay a flat 10% on income above a $10,000 exemption, which for many moderate earners would be a cut, but they would lose every deduction and credit, and the burden of funding the government would shift squarely onto wages.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the corporate income tax and the corporate alternative minimum tax, along with taxes on life insurance companies, other insurers, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts.
Taxes individuals at a flat 10% on earned income above a $10,000 exemption, indexed to inflation — a lower rate than today's brackets for most wage earners.
Excludes pensions and annuities entirely from taxable income, and excludes tips unless they are mandatory, so retirees would owe no income tax.
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes for deaths and transfers after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the federal government would lose the corporate income tax, the estate and gift tax, and most individual income tax revenue, while collecting 10% on wages only. Wage earners above $10,000 in pay would fund the government while investors, corporations, and heirs paid almost nothing — and the lost revenue would have to be made up through borrowing, cuts to programs, or other taxes.

drawbacks.text: Because only wages and self-employment earnings are taxed, capital gains, interest, rents, most dividends, and pensions would be entirely tax-free — a person living entirely off investments would owe nothing, while a worker earning the same amount would owe 10% above $10,000.
Repealing the corporate income tax, the estate and gift tax, and most individual income tax at once would eliminate a large share of federal revenue, with no replacement funding source in the bill.

All specific deductions and credits would be repealed, so taxpayers would lose the standard deduction, the child credit, education and energy credits, and other tax breaks they rely on, replaced only by the $10,000 exemption.

A good-faith supporter would argue the bill simplifies the tax code and ends the double taxation of corporate profits — but the simplification comes entirely by removing taxes on corporations and capital, not by spreading them around.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward redistribution of the tax burden away from corporations, investment income, and inherited wealth, and onto paychecks. Some moderate wage earners would pay less, but the sweeping loss of revenue from repealing corporate and estate taxes is nowhere offset in the bill, and the complete tax exemption of investment income would let the wealthiest households pay nothing while workers fund the government.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Helms introduced it with zero cosponsors in January 1993; it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever considered it and no vote was ever held before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jesse Helms introduced the Flat Tax Act of 1993 on January 26, 1993, with introductory remarks in the Senate.

The bill was read a second time on March 3, 1993, and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders, where it remained without a committee hearing, floor debate, or vote through the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, nothing changed: the existing progressive income tax, corporate income tax, and estate tax remained in place, so corporations, investors, and large estates continued to pay taxes they would have been relieved of. Wage earners kept their deductions and credits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; corporations and estates kept paying

for.name: Sen. Jesse Helms
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Carolina, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 26, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks; it never moved past the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senators cosponsored the bill, so no partisan pattern can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax and the corporate minimum tax entirely, eliminating taxes on corporate profits. Shareholders would capture the benefit while the lost revenue would fall on wage earners and federal programs.

The tax applies only to earned income, so capital gains, interest, rents, most dividends, and pensions would be untaxed — households living off investments would owe essentially nothing. The estate and gift tax repeal would also let large estates pass to heirs untaxed.

industries.industry: Life insurers, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill repeals the specific taxes on life insurance companies, other insurers, mutual funds, and REITs, removing taxes on financial sectors that ordinary savers and taxpayers would no longer help fund through those channels.

Workers would pay a flat 10% above a $10,000 exemption — lower than current rates for many — but they would lose every deduction and credit and would effectively bear the tax burden shifted away from corporations and capital.
